background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: I'm curious about your thoughts about the concern over police conduct, especially when we see shootings of what appear to be unarmed people. Do you think that there is something to be learned from this, that police can do their jobs differently to reduce these encounters?

ground_truth: No, I think the common denominator really is resistance to police. I'm not saying that if one resists police, then anything goes. But all of these episodes, or virtually every one of them, start with physical resistance to the police, and things get out of control. Also, the number of unarmed people shot is very small compared to all the encounters. Because of the number of guns in this country and the high crime rates in this country, we have a high volume of contact between police and violators. And yet, last year, there were nine African Americans who were unarmed who were shot by white police officers. And I think there were a total of 40 or so, maybe, nationwide of people shot who were unarmed. But in that range, it's small. But even there, in many cases, those individuals were fighting with the police and attacking the police officer.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_01
background.text: But would you favor what some police executives have talked about is more training for de-escalation, where it seems in the minds of many that if you don't obey a policeman's command, they just keep upping the force until you do. Is there some advantage to so-called de-escalation training, do you think?

ground_truth: I think police, by and large, do de-escalation from the very moment they encounter people. I know that it's become a buzzword, hey, we need to do more de-escalation, but that's what police do. They try to de-escalate, and it's basically trying to give an opportunity to a person to comply and trying to get them to comply without using force. Police are not out there to necessarily start physical confrontation and get into fights with people. People have to remember something. The police officer doesn't have the luxury of walking away. He can't say, oh, you don't want to be arrested today? I'll see you some other time. When someone resists, they have to obtain compliance, and they usually try to do it verbally without physicality. But obviously de-escalation has been, should remain, part of the arsenal, so to speak, of the police in dealing. According to some of the laws, the police don't really deal with potential criminals or suspects. But there's a double standard going on. This is what's happening. Normally we would say, wait until all the facts are in before you judge somebody. But that's not happening for police officers. The prosecutors frequently don't put out all the facts in a shooting, and the media piles on right away with the most nefarious interpretation of events and usually picks up the facts. up the chant of extremists who have an axe to grind against the police. So a police officer is personally demonized and the episode is frequently mischaracterized from the beginning and the truth never catches up with it. And that's the conundrum that we face in law enforcement. The prosecution holds back the information. Now in the current environment, I think we should get out facts much more quickly to be fair to the police officers.
